title: Medusa and Perseus
subtitle: The gaze that turns you to stone
subject: mythologie
description: Medusa turns anyone who looks at her to stone. Perseus beats her with a mirrored shield, then saves Andromeda. The head of the Gorgon becomes a protective symbol.

hero.hook: A gaze that turns life into stone. A hero who dares to look only at the reflection.

blocks.text: The myth of **Perseus** and **Medusa** is one of the great Greek adventures. It is not only a fight against a monster. It is also the story of beauty turned into horror, and of a hero who wins by cunning.
Medusa, a [[Gorgon]], turns anyone who meets her eyes to stone. To survive, Perseus agrees to look at the danger only through a mirror.

According to Ovid's [[Metamorphoses]], Medusa was not a monster at first. She was a young woman with dazzling hair, a priestess in the temple of **Athena**, goddess of wisdom. Her beauty drew **Poseidon**, god of the seas, who raped her inside the sanctuary.

In the cruel logic of ancient tragedy, Athena punished the victim. Medusa's hair turned into snakes. Her gaze **petrified** anyone who met it. Banished to the edge of the world with her sisters Stheno and Euryale, she lived in a cave ringed with statues: the unlucky men who had seen her.

blocks.caption: Medusa, the Gorgon with the deadly gaze

blocks.text: The blood from Medusa's left side was a deadly poison. The blood from her right side could raise the dead: a secret Athena later passed to **Asclepius**, god of medicine.

sections.title: Perseus arms himself against the impossible

blocks.text: King **Polydectes** wanted Perseus out of the way so he could court his mother **Danae**. He set him a suicidal challenge: bring back the head of Medusa. Perseus was a son of **Zeus**, so the gods helped him.

**Hermes** gave him winged sandals and a [[harpe]], a curved sword with a razor edge. **Hades** lent him the [[Kynee]], a helmet of invisibility. Athena offered the decisive advice: use her polished bronze shield as a **mirror**.

blocks.caption: Perseus approaches Medusa looking only at her reflection

blocks.text: Perseus caught Medusa asleep. Guided by the reflection, he cut off her head. From the neck sprang [[Pegasus, born from Medusa's blood]] and the giant [[Chrysaor]]. Medusa had still been pregnant by Poseidon.

The head kept its power. Perseus stowed it in the [[Kibisis]], a magic pouch. Flying over Ethiopia, he saw the princess **Andromeda** chained to a rock. She had been offered to **Cetus**, a sea monster sent by Poseidon to punish the pride of her mother Cassiopeia.

blocks.caption: Perseus frees Andromeda with the head of Medusa

blocks.text: Some legends say Perseus created red coral by laying the head of Medusa on seaweed: the blood is supposed to have hardened the plants.
Perseus turned the monster to stone, married Andromeda, then sailed home to Seriphos. In front of Polydectes and his court, he drew out the head. His enemies became statues. The tyranny was over.

sections.title: The Gorgoneion, a face that protects

blocks.text: Perseus handed the head to Athena. She fixed it on her **aegis**, her divine shield. Medusa went from monster to be killed to protective power. That emblem, the [[Gorgoneion]], decorated Greek temples, coins and shields.

Its function is [[Apotropaic]]: to turn evil away through the sheer horror of the face. Over the centuries Medusa also became a tragic figure, then a modern icon of trauma, power and fascination. Even the house of Versace picked her head as a logo, to “petrify” the eye.
**Perseus** defeated **Medusa** using the reflection in a shield. The head, handed to **Athena**, became the **Gorgoneion**, the protective symbol of ancient Greece.
